name: Circuits
title: Series, parallel, Kirchhoff and building blocks
intro: Once you know parts, you wire them. These lessons cover series and parallel networks, Kirchhoff's laws, dividers, RC timing, filter intuition, a first look at amplifiers, and how to read a schematic without getting lost.

lessons.title: Series circuits
lessons.summary: One path: shared current, voltages add.

sections.p: In a series circuit, components share one current path. The same current flows through each part. Voltages across the parts add up to the source voltage (Kirchhoff's voltage law in a single loop).
R_total = R1 + R2 + … Two 1 kΩ in series make 2 kΩ. Stringing resistors raises resistance and shares voltage.
If any series element goes open, the whole loop stops. Christmas lights of old failed this way when one bulb opened.

sections.p: In a parallel circuit, components share the same two nodes — the same voltage appears across each branch. Branch currents add to the total supply current.
1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … Two equal resistors in parallel make half the resistance. Two 1 kΩ in parallel → 500 Ω.
Every module on a 5 V rail is roughly in parallel on that rail. Total current is the sum of module currents. Undersized supplies brown out when the sum exceeds rating.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's laws
lessons.summary: KCL and KVL as bookkeeping for circuits.

sections.p: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): the sum of currents into a node equals the sum leaving it (charge does not pile up at an ideal node). Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): the signed sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero.
If 20 mA enters a node and 5 mA leaves on one wire, 15 mA must leave on the others combined. Power-rail planning is KCL with bigger numbers.
From battery + through drops and back: all drops account for the battery rise. If your calculated drops do not close the loop, a sign or a missing element is wrong.
Pick a loop direction and stick to it. Crossing a resistor with current gives a voltage drop that way; a source rise depends on whether you go − to + or the reverse.

KCL: Σ I_in = Σ I_out
KVL: Σ V_loop = 0

lessons.title: Voltage and current dividers
lessons.summary: Tapping a fraction of a voltage or steering current.

sections.p: A resistive voltage divider makes a lower voltage from a higher one: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2) when R2 is the grounded leg and almost no current is drawn from the tap.
If something draws current from the tap, the divider equation changes. Keep the load resistance much larger than the divider resistors, or buffer with an op-amp / use a regulator.
Vin = 5 V, R1 = 10 kΩ (top), R2 = 20 kΩ (bottom) → Vout = 5 × 20/30 ≈ 3.33 V. Handy for level hints — still check ADC loading.
Parallel resistors split current inversely to resistance: the smaller resistor takes more current. Two equal branches split current equally.

Vin ---[R1]---+--- Vout
             |
            [R2]
             |
            GND

Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1+R2)  (unloaded)

lessons.title: RC timing
lessons.summary: Charging curves and the time constant τ = R C.

sections.p: A resistor feeding a capacitor creates an RC circuit. The time constant τ = R C (ohms × farads = seconds). After about one τ, a charging capacitor toward a fixed voltage reaches ~63% of the final value; after ~5τ it is essentially settled.
R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 nF → τ = 10e3 × 100e-9 = 1 ms. Useful for debounce, reset timing, and simple delays (crystal clocks are better when you need accuracy).
The same τ governs discharge toward 0 V through R. Scope the curve: it is exponential, not a straight ramp (unless current is forced constant).
Larger R or larger C slows the transient. That is how you soften edges or hold a supply up briefly — within limits of leakage and load.

lessons.title: Filters intuition
lessons.summary: Letting some frequencies through, attenuating others.

sections.p: A filter favours some frequencies over others. A series resistor and shunt capacitor to ground is a simple low-pass: slow changes appear at the output; fast spikes are shorted by the capacitor.
Swap the roles: series capacitor and shunt resistor passes fast edges / AC and blocks steady DC — useful for coupling audio while rejecting DC bias.
For a first-order RC low-pass, f_c ≈ 1 / (2π R C). R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF → f_c ≈ 160 Hz. Order-of-magnitude thinking beats false precision on a breadboard.
ADC anti-alias RC, EMI ferrites, speaker crossovers, radio IF chains. Start by asking: do I want to keep slow, keep fast, or keep a band?

lessons.title: Amplifiers intro
lessons.summary: Making a small signal larger — with power from a supply.

sections.p: An amplifier takes a small input and produces a larger output, using energy from a power supply. Gain might be voltage gain Vout/Vin. A transistor stage or an op-amp IC are common building blocks.
An ideal op-amp has huge gain, tiny input current, and is used with feedback. In negative feedback, the output moves so the inputs stay nearly equal — that is how we set precise gains with resistors.
With R1 from − input to ground and Rf from output to − input, gain ≈ 1 + Rf/R1 (ideal). Example: Rf = 9 kΩ, R1 = 1 kΩ → gain ≈ 10.
Outputs cannot exceed the supply rails (and often cannot reach them fully). Slew rate and bandwidth limit fast signals. Clipping sounds harsh in audio and ruins measurement peaks.

Non-inverting (ideal):

           >---- Vout
      +--> -/   |

lessons.title: Reading schematics
lessons.summary: Symbols, nets, and finding your way on a diagram.

sections.p: A schematic shows electrical connections with symbols, not physical layout. Wires that meet at a dot are connected; crossing wires without a dot are not (styles vary — check the drawing rules).
R12 is a resistor, C3 a capacitor, U1 an IC, Q1 a transistor, J1 a connector, D4 a diode. Values sit beside the symbol: 10k, 100n, 0.1µF.
Named nets like +3V3, GND, SDA connect across pages without drawing spaghetti. Same name means same node. Ground symbols usually tie together unless multiple grounds are explicitly separated.
Find the power rails first, then the MCU or central IC, then peripherals. Trace one signal: where it starts, what series parts it hits, where it ends.

lessons.title: Thévenin intuition
lessons.summary: Replacing a network with Vth and Rth.

sections.p: Thévenin's theorem says that from the point of view of one load, a linear network of sources and resistors can be replaced by one voltage Vth in series with one resistance Rth. That is why "looking into" a divider matters.
Unloaded divider Vout is Vth. Rth is what you measure at the tap with sources zeroed (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened): for two resistors, Rth = R1 ∥ R2.
If Rload ≫ Rth, the tap barely sags. If Rload ≈ Rth, you lose half the voltage to Rth. ADC pins, comparator inputs and scopes all load the node a little.
Every real signal source has some Rth (output impedance). Cables and op-amp outputs are not perfect stiff voltage sources.

sections.code:
Network  ≡  Vth ---[Rth]--- tap ---- Rload ---- GND

Divider: Vth = Vin*R2/(R1+R2),  Rth = R1||R2
